claims.text: The investigated alloy has nominal composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting alloy is additively manufactured.
The as-fabricated alloy has a homogeneous fcc matrix.
The as-fabricated alloy has minimal pre-existing surface oxide.
The starting alloy has high strength and fatigue performance.
A controlled comparison should expose identical specimens at 750 °C in oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
An exposure duration of 10–50 hours is sufficient for relevant oxide-scale formation or degradation.
High-temperature degradation is governed by the formation and stability of a protective multicomponent oxide scale.
In oxidizing gas, Al, Ti, and Cr become enriched at the surface and form a dense, adherent oxide scale.
The protective oxide is predominantly a mixture of Al2O3 and TiO2.
A coherent multicomponent oxide scale retards oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Reduced oxygen ingress preserves the underlying fcc structure and mechanical performance.
Under reducing conditions, the protective scale fails to form or becomes non-protective through partial reduction, volatile suboxide formation, or increased porosity.
Failure of the scale under reducing conditions enhances oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Enhanced oxygen diffusion causes grain-boundary oxidation or internal oxidation.
Internal oxidation and associated microstructural degradation reduce strength and fatigue life.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a stable, thicker, adherent scale and less internal degradation than reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will retain high strength and fatigue resistance relative to the as-fabricated baseline, whereas reducing exposure will degrade those properties.
The proposed oxidation mechanism applies at approximately 750 °C or above.
Secondary-phase or precipitate evolution during aging may influence the degradation response.

contradictions.description: The reducing comparison includes a highly inert atmosphere with minimal oxygen, yet the mechanism predicts enhanced oxygen ingress and more internal oxidation in that condition. Without fixing oxygen partial pressure or introducing a prior oxide, minimal oxygen availability conflicts with the predicted oxidation-driven degradation.

H2-rich gas and highly inert gas with trace oxygen are treated as equivalent reducing environments, although they can differ substantially in oxygen potential, oxide reduction behavior, and volatile-species formation.
